\chapter{Family}
\label{ch:la-family}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my father, mother, brother, and sister in Latin, and say why Spanish stopped using frāter.}

Name the four household members aloud, then trace frāter germānus down to Spanish hermano.

\section[pater, mater]{pater, mater — the oldest words, kept close to the source}

\label{lesson:LA-C07-pater-mater}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Father\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{} are among the \textbf{oldest reconstructible words in human language}. Latin kept them almost exactly as they were; English took the very same ancestor down a different road.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pater} (\textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{\textbf{ph\textsubscript{2}t\'{\={e}}r}}.
  \item \textbf{māter} (\textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{\textbf{méh\textsubscript{2}tēr}}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Here's the point worth getting exactly right: \textbf{pater and English father are not one derived from the other.} Both descend \textbf{independently, in parallel}, from the same PIE word. Latin simply kept the ancestral \textbf{p} and \textbf{t} close to unchanged; the Germanic branch that produced English took a separate route through \textbf{Grimm's Law}, which shifted that same inherited \textbf{p $\to$ f} and \textbf{t $\to$ th}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{PIE ancestor} & \textbf{Latin} & \textbf{Germanic $\to$ English} \\
\midrule
\emph{ph\textsubscript{2}t\'{\={e}}r} & \textbf{pater} & \textbf{f}a\textbf{th}er \\
\emph{méh\textsubscript{2}tēr} & \textbf{māter} & \textbf{m}o\textbf{th}er \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{pater} and \emph{father} are \textbf{siblings}, sharing one parent-word thousands of years back — not a case of English borrowing or descending from Latin. \emph{Pater} also gives Latin (and later English, through Latin) the whole \textquotedblleft{}of-a-parent\textquotedblright{} family: \textbf{paternus} (\textquotedblleft{}fatherly,\textquotedblright{} $\to$ English \emph{paternal}) and \textbf{māternus} ($\to$ \emph{maternal}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pater, māter\textquotedblright{} — father, mother
  \item the relationship — \textquotedblleft{}cousins, not ancestor and descendant\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pater $\to$ paternus $\to$ paternal; māter $\to$ māternus $\to$ maternal\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does English \emph{father} come \textbf{from} Latin \emph{pater}? (\textbf{No} — both descend \textbf{independently} from the same PIE word, \emph{ph\textsubscript{2}t\'{\={e}}r}.) What sound-law explains the difference between them? (\textbf{Grimm's Law} — the Germanic branch shifted the inherited p $\to$ f, t $\to$ th; Latin kept them.) What Latin adjectives give English \emph{paternal} and \emph{maternal}? (\textbf{Paternus, māternus}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[frater, soror]{frater, soror — Latin's original siblings, before Spanish moved on}

\label{lesson:LA-C07-frater-soror}



\begin{quote}
Two more ancient words — and a preview of a twist: these are the very words that later got \textbf{pushed aside} in everyday Latin, on the road to Spanish.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{frāter} (\textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{\textbf{b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr}}.
  \item \textbf{soror} (\textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{\textbf{swésōr}}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Same rule as \emph{pater/māter}: \textbf{frāter is not the source of English \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{}} — they're \textbf{cousins}, both from \emph{b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr}, with Grimm's Law shifting the Germanic branch's \textbf{b\textsuperscript{h} $\to$ b} while Latin developed its own \textbf{f} (from an earlier \emph{b\textsuperscript{h} $\to$ f} shift already inside Latin itself).

\textbf{Soror} is the more surprising one. English \textbf{sister} looks nothing like \emph{soror} — and that's because Latin \textbf{dropped} the \emph{w} from the PIE cluster \emph{sw-} (giving plain \emph{s-}), while the Germanic branch \textbf{kept} the \emph{w} far longer (Old English had \emph{sweostor}). So \emph{soror} and \emph{sister} are, once again, \textbf{cousins from the same PIE word}, \emph{swésōr} — neither one turned into the other; each branch just handled that opening \emph{sw-} differently.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's the twist: classical Latin could say \textbf{frāter germānus}, \textquotedblleft{}a brother \textbf{of the same blood},\textquotedblright{} to mark a \emph{full} sibling. Over time, in everyday (Vulgar) Latin, that \textbf{adjective} \emph{germānus} took over the whole job, and \textbf{frāter itself faded out of common use} — which is exactly why Spanish says \textbf{hermano}, not a descendant of \emph{frāter} at all. (French \emph{frère} took the opposite path and kept \emph{frāter} as its everyday word — different Latin regions, different survivors.)
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}frāter, soror\textquotedblright{} — brother, sister
  \item the cousin relationship — \textquotedblleft{}frāter/brother and soror/sister are BOTH parallel descendants, not one from the other\textquotedblright{}
  \item the twist — \textquotedblleft{}frāter germānus\textquotedblright{} $\to$ just \textquotedblleft{}germānus\textquotedblright{} $\to$ Spanish \textquotedblleft{}hermano\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is English \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{} descended from Latin \emph{soror}? (\textbf{No} — both are cousins from PIE \emph{swésōr}; Latin dropped the \emph{w}, Germanic kept it longer.) What Latin phrase eventually replaced \emph{frāter} in everyday speech, and where does it show up today? (\emph{\textbf{Frāter germānus}} $\to$ just \emph{germānus} $\to$ Spanish \textbf{hermano}.) Did every Romance language make that same swap? (\textbf{No} — French kept \emph{frāter} as \emph{frère}; Spanish moved on to \emph{germānus}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
